data.title: Course map, sources and how to use this study guide
data.subtitle: History of Uzbekistan

narr: Welcome to the History of Uzbekistan course. Let's start by understanding the structure and expectations of this module.
This is a compulsory course at Tashkent Technological University's Faculty of Power Engineering. It's worth 4 ECTS credits and runs in the autumn semester of 2026/2027.
The course is coordinated by Dr Vohid Kholov and requires a total workload of 120 hours, including 30 contact hours of lectures and 90 hours of independent work.
Assessment includes a midterm exam worth 30%, a project presentation worth 20%, and a final exam worth 50%. The grading scale ranges from A for excellent to D for unsatisfactory.
To be eligible for the final exam, students must attend at least 75% of classes.
The planned learning outcomes focus on understanding, analysis, selection, evaluation, and application of historical concepts and methods.
Here's a breakdown of how your performance will be evaluated in this course.
The midterm exam will test your understanding of the first five learning outcomes.
For the project presentation, you'll work in small groups to present historical processes both in writing and orally.
The final exam carries the most weight at 50% of your total grade.
Remember, you need to attend at least 75% of classes to qualify for taking the final exam.

narr: The course is divided into four weeks, each with specific topics and corresponding course files.
In week one, you'll explore the fundamental subject matter of history as an academic discipline.
Week two focuses on Central Asian civilization and early technological achievements that shaped the region.
Week three examines the history of Uzbek statehood and the formation of the Republic of Uzbekistan.
Finally, week four covers Uzbekistan's path to independence and the challenges of state building that followed.

data.title: Week 1 — The Subject Matter of History
data.subtitle: Understanding history as a science and academic discipline

narr: Now let's dive into week one, which explores the fundamental nature of history as both a science and an academic discipline.
This week addresses key questions about what history is, its nature, its types and auxiliary disciplines, and how historians verify information reliability.
All the propositions, questions, tests, and terms for this week are based on the lecture materials and slides.

data.heading: Key Points: The Definition of History
bullets: History is the study of society's life in the past in all its aspects
Connected with the present and expectations of the future
The story of man in time, based on evidence
Evidence/fact is the "raw material" of history
History is an attempt to re-think the past: what happened, when, and how

narr: Let's explore the fundamental definition of history as presented in this week's materials.
History encompasses the study of human society throughout time, examining all aspects of life in the past.
It connects the past with our present and future expectations, helping us understand how we got here.
At its core, history is the story of humanity across time, built upon evidence and facts.
These facts serve as the raw material that historians use to reconstruct and interpret the past.
Ultimately, history represents our collective attempt to make sense of what happened, when it happened, and how it unfolded.

data.heading: Purpose of Historical Study
bullets: Understanding modern social, political, religious and economic conditions
Provides basis for understanding religion, customs, institutions and governance
Reveals cause-and-effect connections between past and present
Enables accurate and objective understanding of national and international problems

narr: The purpose of studying history extends beyond simple knowledge of the past.
It helps us understand the modern social, political, religious, and economic conditions that shape our world today.
Without historical knowledge, we lack the foundation for comprehending religion, customs, institutions, and systems of governance.
History reveals the cause-and-effect connections between past events and present circumstances.
This understanding enables us to analyze national and international issues with greater accuracy and objectivity.

data.text: History is the record of what one age finds worthy of note in another.

narr: Historians have offered various perspectives on what history truly means.
Burckhardt suggests that history reflects what each generation considers important from the past.

data.text: History in its widest sense is everything that has ever happened.

narr: Henry Johnson takes a broader view, defining history as encompassing all past events.
This perspective emphasizes the comprehensive nature of historical study.

data.text: The value and interest of history depend on the extent to which the present is illuminated by the past.

narr: Smith highlights the practical value of history in understanding our present circumstances.
The usefulness of history depends on how well it helps us illuminate our current situation.

data.text: History is a connected account of the course of events or of the progression of ideas.

narr: Rapson emphasizes the connected nature of historical events and ideas.
History shows how events and concepts develop and relate to one another over time.

data.text: History is the scientific study of past events in all aspects of the life of a social group in the light of what is happening in the present.

narr: NCERT defines history as a scientific study of past events, considering present contexts.
This definition positions history as a systematic discipline that examines social groups comprehensively.

data.text: History is the story of man's struggle through the ages against nature and the elements; against wild beasts and the jungle and against those of his own kind who tried to keep him down and exploit him.

narr: Jawaharlal Nehru offers a more humanistic perspective, focusing on humanity's ongoing struggles.
This view emphasizes the challenges humans have faced throughout history, both from nature and from each other.

data.text: From history we know which ruler was cruel and who held the banner of justice; the qualities and shortcomings of every person are recorded in history.

narr: Alisher Navoi highlights history's role in recording human character and leadership qualities.
History serves as a record of both justice and cruelty, preserving the actions and qualities of individuals.

data.text: Knowledge of the history of the homeland is necessary for every inhabitant.

narr: Ibrat emphasizes the importance of historical knowledge for all members of society.
This perspective suggests that understanding one's homeland history is essential for citizenship.
